mainTopic: Why can't a person testify about a field in someone else's hands? The robber explanation fails, and the גמרא replaces it with a seller's creditor.
overview: The גמרא is checking רב ששת's explanation of a ברייתא: someone whose field was stolen cannot testify for the buyer of that field, but he can testify for the buyer of a stolen cow or cloak. First it asks why the ברייתא does not simply talk about the גזלן himself. It answers that the סיפא needs a sale, which brings יאוש and שינוי רשות, so the רישא also speaks of a sale. Then it objects that the victim still wants the item's value, and answers that the case is where the גזלן died, since his children do not have to pay. Next it asks why the case is not about the גזלן's יורש, and shows that the answer works only for the opinion that an heir's possession is not like a buyer's. אביי adds that the ברייתא's wording about אחריות does not fit the robber explanation at all. So the גמרא drops it and explains the ברייתא with רבין בר שמואל's rule in the name of שמואל: a seller cannot testify about a field he sold, even without a guarantee, because his creditor can collect from it. This applies only to a house or a field, not to a cow or a cloak, and a 'לא מיבעיא' point begins that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why not make the case about the robber himself?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא speaks about testifying for a buyer, when it could simply speak about testifying for the גזלן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the ברייתא be about the robber himself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the way the ברייתא is set up. If the victim is biased about a stolen field, why bring a buyer into the picture at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב ששת, the victim cannot testify because he wants the field to end up somewhere he can take it back from. That reason would work just as well if he were testifying for the גזלן himself. So why does the ברייתא choose the more complicated case of a buyer?

keyTerms.meaning: And let [the ברייתא] be set up as / be explained as
A robber

phrases.english: And let it be set up with regard to the robber!
phrases.notes: He means: why talk about a buyer? Just make the case about testifying for the robber himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case setting of the ברייתא as רב ששת explained it, discussed just before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The choice to set the ברייתא's case about a buyer from the גזלן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same bias exists when testifying for the גזלן himself, so the simpler case should have been used.

steps.title: The second half needs a sale, so the first half has one too
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא speaks of a sale because its סיפא (cow or cloak) only works with a sale. To keep both halves parallel, the רישא also uses a sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the ברייתא wants to teach the סיפא: 'he sold him a cow, he sold him a cloak.' There, a sale is required, because a sale creates יאוש together with שינוי רשות. But if he did not sell it, the item goes back to the victim, so he could not testify. That is why the רישא also says 'sold.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the buyer case was chosen for the sake of the סיפא. With movable items, only a sale makes the victim unbiased.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a cow or cloak, the victim's יאוש plus the change of owner through the sale means he can never take the item back, so he has no interest in the case. If the robber still held it, the victim could take it back, so he would still be biased. The רישא about the field was written with 'sold' just so the two halves match.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter clause of a משנה or ברייתא
The first clause of a משנה or ברייתא
The owner giving up hope of getting his item back
A change of ownership, when the item passes to someone else
Specifically, exactly this case

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the field case itself needs a sale. Land is never lost to its owner through theft. The word 'sold' in the רישא is only there to match the סיפא.

phrases.english: Because he wants to teach the latter clause:

phrases.aramaic: מָכַר לוֹ פָּרָה, מָכַר לוֹ טַלִּית –
phrases.english: He sold him a cow, he sold him a cloak,
where it must specifically be that he sold it,
because then there is despair and a change of possession;
phrases.notes: Together these two mean the victim can no longer take the item back.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לֹא מָכַר, דְּהָדְרָא לֵיהּ – לָא;
phrases.english: but if he did not sell it, so it goes back to him, no;
so he taught the first clause also with 'sold.'

steps.terutzResolutionType: Parallel wording: the רישא copies the case setting the סיפא needs.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer case seemed unnecessary, since the robber case would show the same point.
steps.terutzMaskana: The סיפא needs a sale to create יאוש and שינוי רשות, so the רישא also speaks of a sale to stay parallel.

steps.title: He may have given up on the item, but not on its value
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the סיפא: even after יאוש and a sale, the victim can still demand money from the robber, so he is still biased.
steps.simpleTranslation: And in the סיפא too: granted he gave up on the item itself, did he give up on its value?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. The victim still has a money claim against the robber, so why should he be allowed to testify?
steps.deeperAnalysis: יאוש and שינוי רשות only mean he cannot take the actual cow or cloak back. The robber still owes him its value. So the victim still has a money stake in the outcome, and he still seems biased when he testifies for the buyer.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, even if we accept
He gives up hope
Its value, its price

phrases.english: And the latter clause too:
granted that he gave up hope of the item itself,
did he give up hope of its value?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 2, which said the victim is unbiased in the סיפא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that יאוש and שינוי רשות make the victim unbiased.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The robber still owes the value of the item, so the victim keeps a money interest and is still biased.

steps.title: The case is where the robber died
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the סיפא is speaking about a case where the גזלן has died, so there is no one left to pay the value.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where the robber died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the case of the סיפא to a robber who has died. The next step brings a source showing why that matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the robber is dead, the victim has no one to collect the money from. Now he truly has nothing to gain, so he may testify. The proof for this follows right away.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a specific case)
He died

phrases.english: No, it is needed where the robber died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to a robber who has died.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The victim still has a money claim, so he would still be biased.
steps.terutzMaskana: Once the robber has died, no money can be collected, so the victim is unbiased.

steps.title: Proof: the robber's children do not have to pay
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה: if a robber fed stolen food to his children, or left a stolen item to them, the children do not have to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: one who robs and feeds it to his children, or leaves it to them, they are exempt from paying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the 'robber died' answer with a משנה. After the robber dies, his children do not pay for what he stole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the heirs do not pay, the victim's money claim is gone once the robber dies. That is exactly why he has no interest left and can testify for the buyer.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
One who robs
Exempt from paying

steps.whatToRemember: Movable items: יאוש plus a sale means the item cannot be taken back. Once the robber dies, even its value cannot be collected from his children, so the victim is unbiased.

phrases.english: As we learned:
phrases.notes: This משנה is in בבא קמא קיא:.

phrases.english: One who robs and feeds it to his children,
or left it before them,
they are exempt from paying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 4 with a source.
steps.raayaObject: That after the robber's death the victim cannot collect the value.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in בבא קמא about a robber who feeds stolen food to his children or leaves stolen items to them.

steps.title: Then why not make the case about the robber's heir?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the case is about a dead robber, why not set the whole ברייתא about testifying for his יורש instead of a buyer?
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let the ברייתא be about the heir!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge to the buyer case. Since the robber is dead anyway, testifying for his heir would show the same contrast without needing a sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A stolen field must always go back to its owner, even from the heirs, so the victim is biased there. Step 5 said the heirs do not pay for stolen movables, so it seems he would be unbiased there, and the need for a buyer seems to fall away again. The next step shows this depends on how we view an heir's possession.

keyTerms.meaning: An heir

phrases.english: And let it be set up with regard to the heir!
phrases.notes: He means the robber's heir, since we now said the robber died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the 'robber died' answer to challenge again why the ברייתא needs a buyer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation in step 2 that the buyer case is needed for the סיפא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With the robber dead, an heir case would already make the movable items uncollectable, so no sale and no buyer would be needed.

steps.title: The heir question can be answered for only one opinion
steps.stepSummary: The answer to 'why not an heir?' works only for those who hold an heir's possession is not like a buyer's. For those who hold it is like a buyer's, the question stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the one who says an heir's possession is not like a buyer's possession. But according to the one who says an heir's possession is like a buyer's possession, what can we say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pushing the question from the last step further. It shows there is only a partial way out, and that way out does not work for everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If an heir's possession is not like a buyer's, the stolen item never really 'changed owners', so the victim could still take it back from the heir. That would make him biased, so the ברייתא could not use the heir case. But if an heir's possession does count like a buyer's, the heir case would work just as well, and we are back to asking why the ברייתא chose a sale.

keyTerms.meaning: The possession of an heir: the item is now in the hands of the one who inherited it
The possession of a buyer: the item has passed to a new owner through a sale
This works out well (for this opinion)
What is there to say? This means the current explanation has no good answer, which leads to the new explanation in step 9

steps.confusionAlert: This step does not settle the מחלוקת about heirs. It only shows that the robber explanation depends on one side of it, and that is a weakness.

phrases.english: This works out well according to the one who says:

phrases.aramaic: רְשׁוּת יוֹרֵשׁ לָאו כִּרְשׁוּת לוֹקֵחַ דָּמֵי – שַׁפִּיר;
phrases.english: the possession of an heir is not like the possession of a buyer — fine;
phrases.notes: For this opinion, the stolen item in the heir's hands has not 'changed owners', so the victim could still take it back.

phrases.english: but according to the one who says:
the possession of an heir is like the possession of a buyer —
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sharpens the question of step 6 by showing it can be answered for only one opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The robber explanation of the ברייתא, which says the robber has died
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If an heir's possession counts like a buyer's, the heir case would work just as well, so the ברייתא should not have needed a sale.

steps.title: אביי: the wording of the ברייתא does not fit
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects that if the case is about stolen land, the ברייתא should give the reason as 'it returns to him', not 'the responsibility is on him'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, אביי found it difficult: the ברייתא says 'because the responsibility is on him' and 'the responsibility is not on him'?! It should have said 'because it returns to him' and 'it does not return to him'!
steps.whatsHappening: A second attack on the robber explanation. אביי says the reason the ברייתא gives does not match that explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the robber explanation, the victim is biased because the stolen field comes back to him. A cow or cloak does not come back, because the buyer already owns it. So the ברייתא's reason should have been about getting the item back, not about אחריות (a duty to pay the buyer), which has nothing to do with the victim.

keyTerms.meaning: Responsibility or guarantee: a duty to pay back if the item is taken away
It returns to him (the item goes back to the owner)
It should have said
An אמורא who raises this difficulty

phrases.english: And furthermore, it was difficult for Abaye:
"because the responsibility for it is on him"
phrases.notes: These quoted words are the ברייתא's own reasons for the field case and the cow-or-cloak case.

phrases.english: and "the responsibility for it is not on him"?!
"because it returns to him"
and "it does not return to him" is what it should have said!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, separate attack on the same robber explanation.
steps.kashyaTarget: The robber explanation of the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's stated reason (אחריות) does not match the reason the robber explanation needs (the field returning to the victim).

steps.title: New explanation: the seller keeps the field for his creditor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the robber explanation. It explains the ברייתא with רבין בר שמואל's rule: a seller cannot testify about a field he sold, even without a guarantee, because his creditor can collect from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, explain it like רבין בר שמואל, who said in the name of שמואל: one who sells a field to his fellow without a guarantee cannot testify for him about it, because he is keeping it standing for his creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a whole new explanation of the ברייתא, replacing the robber one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land that a person sold can still be collected by the creditors he owed money to. If the field stays with the buyer, the seller's creditor has something to collect from, which helps the seller. So the seller is biased even without a guarantee, and the ברייתא's 'responsibility' means the seller's duty toward his creditor.

keyTerms.meaning: Without a guarantee: the seller did not promise to pay the buyer back if the field is taken
Testifies
He keeps it standing (keeps the field available)
A creditor, someone the seller owes money to

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא is now explained without any robber: a seller of land is biased because his own creditor can collect from that land.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a seller's bias can come from his own debts, not only from a guarantee he gave the buyer.

phrases.english: Rather, it is like Ravin bar Shmuel —

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רָבִין בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: for Ravin bar Shmuel said in the name of Shmuel:
one who sells a field to his fellow without a guarantee —
cannot testify for him about it,
because he is keeping it standing for his creditor.
phrases.notes: His creditor can collect from land he sold, so he wants the field to stay with the buyer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives up on the robber explanation after the attacks in steps 7 and 8 and offers a new one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New explanation of the ברייתא based on an outside rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was about a robber who sold a stolen field, and the victim was the biased witness.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about an ordinary seller, who is biased because his creditor can collect from the field he sold.

steps.title: Only land, not a cow or a cloak
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits רבין בר שמואל's rule to a house or a field. With a cow or a cloak, a different point begins with 'it is not necessary'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is specifically a house or a field, but a cow or a cloak — no, he is not barred and may testify. It is not necessary to say...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the new rule to land: with a cow or a cloak the seller may testify. It then begins a 'it is not necessary to say' point, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A creditor can collect from land that was sold, but not from movable things like a cow or a cloak. So for movables the seller gains nothing by keeping them with the buyer. The words 'it is not necessary' open a new point that the גמרא finishes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Specifically, only in this case
A cow and a cloak: examples of movable property
It is not necessary (to say), which opens a 'not only this, but even that' point

phrases.english: And this is specifically a house or a field,
but a cow or a cloak —
no [he may testify]; it is not necessary [to say]

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets the limits of the new explanation from step 9 and matches it to the ברייתא's cow-or-cloak case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The creditor-based bias applies only to land (a house or field), not to movables like a cow or a cloak.
